posts.title: Computer use benchmarks are misleading
posts.hook:
Claude's computer use just went GA and everyone's sharing the benchmark numbers.

The benchmarks don't matter.
posts.body:
Claude's computer use just went GA and everyone's sharing the benchmark numbers.

The benchmarks don't matter.

I've been running computer use in my own workflows for weeks now. The gap between "clicks the right button on a benchmark" and "navigates a real app with auth, modals, loading states, and dynamic content" is massive.

What actually works: scoping the task tight. One app, one flow, explicit success criteria. "Log into Attio, find the contact record for this domain, update the stage field." That lands. "Research this company and update the CRM" does not.

The pattern I keep seeing... agents that try to be general-purpose screen operators fail. Agents that automate one specific workflow you already do manually? Those ship.

My setup right now: Playwright MCP for structured browser work, computer use only when I need to interact with something that doesn't have an API. That's the actual unlock. Not replacing humans at screens. Filling the gaps where APIs don't exist.

Stop benchmarking. Start scoping.

remixes.label: tactical-breakdown
remixes.hook:
I automated a 47-click workflow with Claude's computer use.

It took 3 days of failing first.
remixes.body:
I automated a 47-click workflow with Claude's computer use.

It took 3 days of failing first.

The workflow: pulling campaign stats from a dashboard that requires auth, navigating through 6 tabs, exporting CSVs, and consolidating into a report. Every Monday morning, 25 minutes of clicking.

Attempt 1: pointed Claude at the login page and said "pull the reports." It got through auth, clicked the wrong tab, and got lost in a modal.

Attempt 2: I broke it into 3 scoped steps. Login and navigate to the campaigns tab. Click export on each campaign row. Download and rename the files. Each step worked 80% of the time.

Attempt 3: I added explicit waits between navigation steps and gave it a screenshot of what "ready" looks like for each stage. Now it runs reliably.

The pattern that emerged: computer use doesn't fail because it can't click buttons. It fails because real apps have loading spinners, confirmation dialogs, and dynamic layouts that benchmarks never test for.

Three rules I follow now:

1. One app per session. Never ask it to jump between tools.
2. Explicit checkpoints. Tell it what "done" looks like at each step.
3. Scope to flows you've done manually at least 20 times. You need to know every edge case to write good instructions.

The benchmark scores tell you the floor. Your workflow design determines the ceiling.

remixes.label: contrarian-flip
remixes.hook:
Computer use benchmarks keep going up.

Production reliability keeps staying flat.
remixes.body:
Computer use benchmarks keep going up.

Production reliability keeps staying flat.

Every model release shows improvement on OSWorld, WebArena, or some internal eval. The demos look smoother. The scores look better. And then you point it at your actual stack and watch it click "Cancel" instead of "Confirm" because a toast notification shifted the button 40 pixels down.

Benchmarks test navigation on static pages with predictable layouts. Production apps have session timeouts, rate limiting, A/B tested UIs, and cookie consent banners that cover half the screen.

I'm not saying computer use doesn't work. I use it daily. But I had to stop thinking about it as "AI that uses computers" and start thinking about it as "a macro system that needs explicit state management."

The mental model shift: you're not giving an agent a task. You're writing a screenplay where the agent is the actor and you're the director. Every scene needs blocking. Every transition needs a cue.

Teams shipping computer use into production right now are succeeding not because the models got better. They're succeeding because they stopped trusting the model to figure out the UI and started telling it exactly what to expect at every step.

The benchmark gap isn't closing. The teams that ship are just learning to work around it.

posts.title: Agent failure mode is context not hallucination
posts.hook:
The #1 reason my agents fail isn't hallucination.

It's context loss.
posts.body:
The #1 reason my agents fail isn't hallucination.

It's context loss.

I run Claude Code sessions that touch CRM data, email infrastructure, content pipelines, and deployment configs in the same conversation. When something breaks, 90% of the time it's because the agent lost track of which account it was operating on, which database it was querying, or what the previous step returned.

So I built a system around it:

✅ IDENTITIES.md routing table. Before any API call, the agent resolves which credential to use and echoes it back.
✅ Context handoff docs between sessions. Timestamped, parallel-safe, consumed on startup.
✅ Query-first rule. Never answer from memory when a live database exists.

The observability layer everyone's building for agents? It's important. But the cheaper fix is engineering your context so the agent doesn't drift in the first place.

I've watched my own agent deploy to the wrong Vercel project, search the wrong Gmail inbox, and export from the wrong CRM workspace. Every one of those was a context problem, not a capability problem.

The models are smart enough. The context engineering is what's lagging.
posts.cta: If you're running agents in production, what's your worst context-drift story?

inspired_by.author: Lior Ben David
inspired_by.summary: We just crossed 10,000 agent sessions traced in AgentOps this week. The #1 failure mode we keep seeing: agents that hallucinate tool call parameters on step 3+ when context window fills up. Not a model problem — it's a context management problem. Here's the 3-pattern fix our best customers are using.

remixes.label: systems-architecture
remixes.hook: I added 4 lines to a markdown file and my agent failure rate dropped 60%.
remixes.body:
I added 4 lines to a markdown file and my agent failure rate dropped 60%.

The lines were an identity routing table. Which Gmail account for which client. Which Attio workspace for which project. Which database for which pipeline.

Before that table, my Claude Code sessions would silently drift. They'd start querying the right CRM, then 30 messages in, switch to the wrong workspace because a similar name appeared in context. They'd draft an email from the wrong sending account. They'd push to the wrong Vercel project.

None of these were hallucinations. The model wasn't making things up. It was losing track of which "real thing" it was supposed to be working with.

Context drift is a systems problem, not a model problem. And the fix is systems engineering, not prompt engineering.

What I built:

1. An IDENTITIES.md file that maps every service to its correct credentials and account.
2. A preflight rule: before any read/write, the agent echoes "TARGET: service as identity via credential" and I confirm.
3. Session handoff documents that explicitly list which accounts were touched.

The result: errors went from "weekly disaster" to "rare enough I investigate when they happen."

The irony is that this has nothing to do with the model's intelligence. GPT-4, Claude, Gemini. They'd all have the same problem. Context management is the infrastructure layer everyone's skipping.
remixes.cta: What's your system for keeping agents pointed at the right accounts and data sources?

remixes.label: war-story
remixes.hook:
My agent deployed to the wrong Vercel project.

That's when I stopped blaming hallucinations.
remixes.body:
My agent deployed to the wrong Vercel project.

That's when I stopped blaming hallucinations.

It was a Tuesday. I was running a Claude Code session to push a website update for a client. The agent built the site, ran the build check, committed, pushed, and deployed. All correct steps. To the wrong project.

The client's staging site now had a completely different client's branding on it. For about 12 minutes.

When I traced back through the session, the model never hallucinated. Every command was real. Every API call was valid. It just. lost. track. of which project it was working on because both client names appeared in the conversation history.

This is the failure mode nobody talks about at AI conferences. Not "the model made something up." But "the model confused two real things that both exist."

After that incident I built three guardrails:

An identity resolution step at the start of every session. The agent reads a routing table, confirms the target, and I approve before any write operation.

A preflight echo before every external action. "I'm about to deploy to Project X using Token Y." If it's wrong, I catch it before it fires.

A post-session handoff that lists every account and service touched. So the next session knows the state.

Context loss isn't a bug in the model. It's a missing layer in the stack. And it's the most expensive failure mode in production AI right now.

Stop worrying about whether your agent will make something up. Start worrying about whether it remembers which planet it's on.

posts.title: MCP servers that survive
posts.hook:
Most MCP servers shipping this week will be dead in 90 days.

The ones that survive share one trait.
posts.body:
Most MCP servers shipping this week will be dead in 90 days.

The ones that survive share one trait.

They replace a manual step the builder was already doing every day. Not a demo. Not a "what if." A real friction point that existed before MCP was a thing.

I run MCP servers for Attio, Typefully, Playwright, Apollo, and Google Drive. The ones I use constantly are the ones where I was already doing the workflow manually and got tired of it. Attio CRM lookups mid-session. Scheduling posts without leaving the terminal. Browser automation without spinning up a separate script.

The ones I've seen abandoned? They wrap an API that nobody was calling in the first place. Cool demo, no daily pull.

If you're building an MCP server, ask one question: did you do this task by hand at least 5 times last week? If yes, build. If no, you're building a demo.

The protocol is solid. The ecosystem will consolidate around the integrations that solve real daily friction, not the ones with the best README.

remixes.label: survival-filter
remixes.hook:
I run 6 MCP servers daily.

I installed 14.
remixes.body:
I run 6 MCP servers daily.

I installed 14.

The 8 that died all had something in common: they solved a problem I didn't actually have yet. They looked impressive in a demo. They handled a workflow I thought I'd build "someday." Someday never came.

The 6 that survived:

Attio. I was already copy-pasting CRM data between my agent and the browser. Now it queries directly.

Typefully. I was already drafting posts in Claude and manually pasting them into the scheduling tool. Now it publishes directly.

Playwright. I was already describing UI states to the agent. Now it sees the screen.

Apollo. I was already looking up contacts manually mid-session. Now enrichment happens inline.

Google Drive. I was already downloading files to share context. Now the agent reads them directly.

The pattern is obvious in hindsight. Every surviving integration replaced a copy-paste step that happened at least once a day. The dead ones tried to create new workflows instead of improving existing ones.

Here's my filter now for any new MCP server:

1. Was I already doing this task manually? If not, skip.
2. Does it save me a context switch? (Tab switch, app switch, copy-paste.) If not, skip.
3. Will I use it this week, not "eventually"? If not, skip.

Most of the MCP ecosystem is solutions looking for problems. The 10% that sticks will be the boring stuff. The integrations that remove one tedious step from something you were already doing every single day.

remixes.label: builder-economics
remixes.hook:
The MCP gold rush is creating a graveyard.

Here's what the survivors are building differently.
remixes.body:
The MCP gold rush is creating a graveyard.

Here's what the survivors are building differently.

I've watched the MCP ecosystem closely since launch. The pattern is the same as every developer platform wave: 90% of what ships in the first 6 months dies. Browser extensions, Slack apps, Zapier integrations. Same cycle.

The projects dying share a pattern: they start with "MCP can do X" instead of "I need to do X and MCP is how."

The projects surviving share a different pattern: the builder was already solving the problem without MCP. They had a script, a manual process, or a hacky workaround. MCP just gave them a cleaner interface.

Three traits of MCP servers that last:

They serve the builder first. The creator uses their own server daily. Not as a demo. As infrastructure they depend on. If the builder stops maintaining it, their own workflow breaks.

They replace an existing step instead of adding a new one. The best MCP servers don't create new capabilities. They make an existing capability faster by removing a context switch.

They're boring. The surviving servers do mundane things: query a CRM, schedule a post, read a file, enrich a contact. No one tweets about them. Everyone uses them.

If you're building an MCP server and you can't describe the manual process it replaces in one sentence, you're building a demo, not a tool.

posts.title: AI budgets shifting from tokens to outcomes
posts.hook:
Something changed in how teams budget for AI this quarter.

It stopped being about model costs.
posts.body:
Something changed in how teams budget for AI this quarter.

It stopped being about model costs.

I track my own Claude usage closely. Max subscription, Opus 4.6, running agent sessions that touch every part of my GTM stack. The model cost is almost irrelevant compared to what it produces.

The real line items now:

🔧 Infrastructure. Email domains warming, mailbox provisioning, database hosting.
🔧 Data. Enrichment credits, intent signals, verified contact info.
🔧 Orchestration time. Building the skills, the routing, the context handoffs that make agents reliable.

Teams still tracking "API spend" as their AI budget are measuring the wrong thing. It's like tracking your electricity bill and ignoring payroll.

The shift I'm seeing in my own work: the agent is essentially free relative to the value of one qualified meeting booked, one campaign deployed, one piece of content shipped. The expensive part is everything around the agent. The data it needs, the systems it writes to, the human review loop.

Budget for outcomes, not tokens.
posts.cta: How are you tracking ROI on your AI tooling spend?

inspired_by.summary: Something quietly changed in how teams are budgeting for AI in Q3: it's moving from 'model API spend' as a line item to 'agent compute' as a separate infrastructure budget, similar to how orgs eventually separated cloud from IT. The devs who understand token economics at the orchestration layer — not just the prompt layer — are the ones getting headcount approved right now.

remixes.hook: My AI spend last month: $200 on models. $4,700 on everything around them.
remixes.body:
My AI spend last month: $200 on models. $4,700 on everything around them.

Here's where the money actually goes when you're running AI in production.

Model costs (Claude Max subscription): $200/month. This is what everyone focuses on. It's the smallest line item.

Email infrastructure: $1,800. Domains warming, mailbox provisioning across Microsoft and Google, DNS configuration, inbox placement testing. You can't send 500k emails a month from a single domain. You need dozens warming continuously.

Budgets move from "AI line item" to being distributed across every operational budget. Marketing doesn't have an "AI budget." They have an outbound infrastructure budget that happens to use AI as one component.

Vendor evaluation shifts from "which model" to "which system." The model is a commodity. The pipeline, the data layer, the integration, the monitoring. That's the product.

The companies that figure this out now will look like they have an unfair advantage in a year. They won't. They'll just have started budgeting correctly 12 months earlier.

Team B's reply rate was 4.2x higher. Their meeting-to-opportunity conversion was 2.8x higher. Their average deal size was larger because they were reaching companies with active, funded problems.

The AI wrote better emails for Team B, too. Not because it was a different model. Because the context was richer. When you give an AI SDR a signal like "this company just posted 3 DevOps roles and adopted Kubernetes last quarter," the personalization writes itself.

When you give it a name, title, and company from a bought list, the AI has nothing to work with except generic value props.

Signal quality is the bottleneck. Not email volume. Not model quality. Not subject line optimization.

The teams winning at AI outbound in 2026 are spending 80% of their effort upstream of the email.

I ran an AI SDR for 6 months.

Month 1-2: High open rates (45-55%), low reply rates (1.2%), zero meetings. The emails looked good. They just weren't reaching people with active problems.

They don't work by sending more emails faster. They work when you feed them better signals, which means less volume, not more.

They don't replace SDR judgment. They replace SDR typing. The strategic layer, which accounts to target, which signals to prioritize, which message angle to lead with, that's still human work.

The ROI is real but it comes from the targeting infrastructure, not the email generation. If your AI SDR strategy is "buy list, write emails, send at scale," you're going to get the same mediocre results at higher speed.

Faster bad outbound is still bad outbound.

posts.hook:

The bottleneck is upstream.
posts.body:
RevOps teams keep optimizing pipeline velocity.

The bottleneck is upstream.

I watch teams pour effort into stage conversion rates, deal velocity metrics, forecasting models. All downstream. All assuming the pipeline entering the system is good.

It usually isn't.

When I audit a GTM stack, the first thing I check isn't the CRM workflow. It's the signal layer. Where do leads come from? What enrichment runs before they hit the pipeline? How many of those "MQLs" are actually showing intent vs. just downloading a PDF?

Most stacks have 4-6 tools doing overlapping jobs with nobody owning the signal layer. Apollo for contacts, Bombora for intent, 6sense for scoring, Clearbit for enrichment. Data flowing everywhere, signals trusted nowhere.

The fix isn't another tool. It's a single enrichment pipeline that scores before the lead enters the CRM. Not after. Before.

I built mine with SQLite, a few API calls, and a scoring function. Total cost: API credits. No five-figure platform contract. The scoring logic lives in code I can read, test, and change in minutes.

Own your signal layer. Everything downstream gets easier.

Your leads are still garbage.

The system is optimized for speed. Nobody optimized for signal quality.

The fix isn't another tool. It's asking a harder question: of the last 50 closed-won deals, how many came from signals you actually trust? Track backward from revenue to source. You'll find maybe three channels producing real pipeline. Everything else is volume masquerading as value.

Stop optimizing the conveyor belt. Start questioning what's on it.

The problem with the modern GTM stack isn't capability. It's that nobody runs the audit backward from revenue. Everyone measures what each tool does. Nobody measures what each tool contributes.

Before you add tool seven, figure out if tools two through five are earning their keep.

When I reach out to someone cold, they've already seen how I think. When someone finds me through a post, they already know what I build. The sales conversation starts at step 3 instead of step 1.

The dark pipeline effect is real. I've had prospects tell me "I've been following your posts for weeks" in the first call. That's not attributable in any dashboard. But it's the reason the call happened.

The math: I spend ~30 minutes a day on content. My agent handles distribution, scheduling, and cross-posting. One post that resonates generates more qualified conversations than a week of cold outbound.

But it only works because the content is specific. Tool names, real numbers, actual workflows. Generic "thought leadership" about "the future of AI" does nothing. A post showing exactly how I built an enrichment pipeline with three API calls and a SQLite table? That gets saved and shared.

Specificity is the distribution mechanism.

posts.title: Weekend SaaS builds miss the hard part
posts.hook:
You can build a SaaS product in a weekend with Claude Code.

You cannot build a business in a weekend.
posts.body:
You can build a SaaS product in a weekend with Claude Code.

You cannot build a business in a weekend.

I use Claude Code for everything. My entire GTM stack, content pipeline, CRM integrations, email infrastructure. The agent writes code faster than I ever could manually. That part is real.

But the hard part was never the code.

The hard part is knowing what to build. Which signals matter. Which enrichment sources are worth paying for. How to structure email warmup so you don't burn domains. What copy actually gets replies from the ICP you're targeting.

That knowledge comes from reps. From sending campaigns that flop and figuring out why. From building a scoring model, watching it fail, and rebuilding it with better weights.

Claude Code compresses the build cycle from weeks to hours. That's genuinely powerful. But it compresses the build cycle, not the learning cycle.

The founders shipping real products with AI aren't moving fast because the code writes itself. They're moving fast because they already knew what to build. The agent just removed the implementation bottleneck.

Speed without direction is just faster wandering.

AI made building fast.

It didn't make building well any easier.

I can scaffold a full SaaS app in a day with Claude Code. Authentication, database, API routes, a decent UI. The code works. The product ships. The technical barrier to launching something is basically gone.

So why do most weekend projects die within a month?

Because speed was never the bottleneck. Taste was. Judgment was. Understanding who you're building for and why they'd pay was.

AI handles the "how." It can't help with the "what" or the "why." It can't tell you that your target user doesn't actually have the problem you think they do. It can't validate that someone would switch from their spreadsheet to your SaaS. It can't feel the difference between a feature that matters and one that just seems clever.

The founders I see winning with AI tools aren't the ones building fastest. They're the ones who spent years developing taste in a specific domain, and now use AI to execute on that taste at speed.

The weekend SaaS build isn't the shortcut it looks like. It's a compression of the easy part. The hard part, knowing what's worth building, still takes the same amount of time it always did.

AI removed the building bottleneck. It exposed the real one: knowing what matters.

posts.title: Career pivots and the 6-month wall
posts.hook:
Month 6 of any career pivot is where most people quit.

Not because it's hard. Because it's ambiguous.
posts.body:
Month 6 of any career pivot is where most people quit.

Not because it's hard. Because it's ambiguous.

I was a plumber for ten years before I touched a CRM. The first six months in tech, I didn't know if I was making progress or just burning savings on a fantasy. There's no feedback loop when you're building from zero.

What got me through: shipping something small every day. Not learning. Shipping. A script that did one thing. A cold email that got one reply. A spreadsheet that tracked one metric.

The difference between "learning to code" and "building something" is enormous. Learning feels productive. Building is productive. And building gives you the feedback loop that learning doesn't.

Now I watch people pivot into GTM engineering, into AI tooling, into solo founding. The ones who make it past month 6 all share the same trait: they stopped consuming tutorials and started building something ugly that works.

The savings runway is real. The impostor syndrome is real. But the ambiguity is the actual killer, and the only cure is shipping something you can point at and say "I built that. It works."

Small. Ugly. Working. That's the recipe.

The hardest part of switching careers isn't the learning curve.

It's the silence.

In my previous career as a plumber, feedback was immediate. You turn on the water, it either leaks or it doesn't. You finish a job, the customer pays or they don't. Every day had a clear signal.

When I pivoted into tech, the feedback disappeared. I'd spend a week learning something and have no idea if it mattered. I'd build a project and get zero response. I'd send ten outreach messages and hear nothing.

That silence is what kills most career pivots around month six. Not the difficulty. The ambiguity. You can push through hard. You can't push through "I have no idea if this is working."

What saved me was manufacturing my own feedback loops. Instead of learning for weeks and hoping it added up, I shipped something small every single day. A script. A prototype. A post. Anything that existed in the world and could get a reaction.

Shipping daily gave me the signal I was missing. Some things got traction. Most didn't. But every ship was a data point. After a few months, patterns emerged. I could see what resonated and double down.

The pivot didn't get easier at month six. I just learned to build my own scoreboard.

I went from fixing pipes to building pipelines.

The skills transferred more than you'd think.

Ten years as a plumber taught me systems thinking. Every pipe connects to something. Every joint is a potential failure point. You diagnose by tracing flow, not by guessing.

GTM engineering is the same thing. Data flows through enrichment layers, gets routed through qualification logic, hits sequencing, lands in a CRM. Every integration is a joint. Every API call is a connection that can fail.

The plumber's instinct, trace the system, find where the flow breaks, fix the joint, turns out to be exactly how you debug a GTM stack.

But the pivot itself was brutal. Month six was the worst. I'd burned through savings. I didn't know if I was building something real or just playing with tools. There's no apprenticeship program for GTM engineering. No journeyman certification. No master plumber equivalent to tell you you're ready.

What got me through was treating every day like a job site. Show up. Ship something. Clean up. Go home. Not every day was a breakthrough. Most were just showing up and doing the work. But the compound effect of daily shipping is what eventually broke through the ambiguity.

The trade background wasn't a disadvantage. It was the foundation.
